Inductance From a Field Solve

ENEL 585, Topic 13 (Magnetics). Optional self-study: how to get L from the magnetic field with FEMM, and why it comes out about 13 % above the lecture's formula.

What you need: FEMM 4.2, free from femm.info (Windows). The finished model, core-inductor.fem, is posted beside this page. Open it in FEMM and press Analysis → Analyze to skip straight to step 5.

The core: the lecture's example: N = 40 turns, μr = 2000, Ac = 1 cm², mean path ℓc = 100 mm. The lecture's formula gives

L ≈ μrμ0AcN²/ℓc = 4.02 mH.

That formula takes the field to be the same everywhere in the core. A field solver like FEMM makes no such assumption: it finds the actual field.

The model

FEMM solves a 2D cut of the core. Here the cut is taken at mid-depth and seen from the front. The core is 35 × 27 mm with 6 mm legs, so the mean path is 2(29 + 21) = 100 mm. The winding on the left leg shows up in the cut as two copper strips:

  • one in the window, where the current goes into the page;
  • one beside the leg's outer face, where the same wire comes back out of the page.

FEMM treats the cut as repeated over a depth d = 100/6 = 16.7 mm, so Ac = 6 mm × 16.7 mm = 1 cm². The current is i = 0.1 A, so N i = 4 A.

Step 0: a new problem

File → New → Magnetics Problem, then Problem → Problem Definition: Problem Type Planar, Length Units Millimeters, Frequency 0, Depth 16.667.

Frequency 0 makes it a static (magnetostatic) problem, so there are no eddy currents. Planar means the cut is repeated over the depth.

Step 1: draw the outlines

Draw the core's outer edge, the window, and the two copper strips (each 1.5 mm wide, 0.4 mm from the leg). Use Operate on nodes to place corners (press Tab to type coordinates), then Operate on segments to join them. FEMM only knows regions enclosed by lines.

Step 2: say what each region is

Each region gets one block label, which sets its material and mesh size and, for copper, its circuit and number of turns.

  • Properties → Materials: add Core (linear, μx = μy = 2000), Air (μ = 1) and Copper (μ = 1).
  • Properties → Circuits: add coil, 0.1 A, Series. Every turn carries the same current, so the whole winding is one circuit.
  • In Operate on block labels mode, click inside each region, then right-click it and press Space to set its properties. The window strip gets circuit coil with −40 turns, because FEMM counts current out of the page as positive and here it goes in. The outer strip gets +40.

Step 3: an open boundary

A little of the field spreads into the air, and real air goes on forever. FEMM's Create open boundary button adds rings around the model (here 7 layers, radius 140 mm) that make its edge act as if it did.

7 layers at 140 mm (4 × the core's width) is a safe default, not a requirement. For this core it hardly matters: a single layer, or a radius of 70 mm or 280 mm, gives the same L to 0.01 %, because almost all the flux stays inside the core. It matters more when much of the field is in the air, as with a gapped or air-core inductor. There, double the radius and check L does not move.

Step 4: mesh

Mesh → Create Mesh. FEMM splits every region into small triangles and solves for the field at their corners. Smaller triangles give a more exact answer. This model uses 0.25 mm triangles in the core and copper and coarser ones in the air. Making them 0.1 mm changes L by only 0.03 %.

Step 5: solve and look at the field

Analysis → Analyze, then Analysis → View Results, and turn on the density plot of |B|. FEMM has found the field that obeys Ampère's law on every loop and B = μrμ0H in every triangle.

The black lines are flux lines, with equal flux between neighbours. They bunch against the inside corners (pink, above 0.14 T) and thin out toward the outside corners. The flux takes the short way round.

Step 6: read the inductance

What flux linkage λ is

One turn of wire is a loop, and some flux Φ1 passes through it. Faraday's law for that loop: v1 = dΦ1/dt.

40 turns in series: their voltages add,

v = dΦ1/dt + … + dΦ40/dt = dλ/dt,   λ = Φ1 + Φ2 + … + Φ40.

λ, the flux linkage, is the flux through each turn added over all the turns, in webers. If every turn has the same flux Φ, then λ = NΦ. That is the lecture's v = N Ac dB/dt, with λ = N B Ac.

From λ to L: every material here is linear, so doubling i doubles λ. So λ = L i, which gives v = L di/dt and

L = λ / i.

What a turn is in the 2D cut

A turn shows up as two dots: the wire going into the page in the window, and coming back out beside the leg. The flux through that turn is the flux crossing a line between the two dots, which is the flux in the wound leg.

From B to flux

To get the flux crossing the red line, add up B along it, with two refinements:

  1. Only the part of B that crosses the line counts: here the vertical component, By.
  2. Each B is weighted by the area it covers. A piece of the line Δx wide stands for a strip Δx wide and d deep, so its flux is ByΔx d:

    Φ = d Σ ByΔx  →  Φ = d ∫ By dx.

If B is the same all the way across, this is just Φ = B Ac. In general, Φ = (average B across Ac) × Ac.

across the 6 mm wound leg, at mid-heightBy
near the outer faceabout 0.112 T
middleabout 0.113 T
near the windowabout 0.115 T
average0.1133 T

0.1133 T × 1 cm² = 11.33 µWb. In FEMM you can do this sum yourself: draw the line as a contour, then Integrate → Line Integral → B.n.

Reading λ and L in FEMM

View → Circuit Props, then pick coil. FEMM adds up the flux through all 40 turns (Flux linkage) and divides by the current (Flux/Current, which is L).

lecture's formulaFEMM
B in the wound leg0.1005 T everywhere0.1133 T on average
flux through each turn, λ/N10.05 µWb11.32 µWb
λ0.402 mWb0.453 mWb
L = λ/i4.02 mH4.53 mH

Step 7: check the answer

Ampère on the mean path. Draw the mean path as a contour (Operation → Contour, click the four corners), then Integrate → Line Integral → H.t. It should give N i = 4 A; FEMM gives 4.0002 A.

Dividing by the path's length gives the average H along it: 4 A / 0.1 m = 40 A/m, exactly N i/ℓc. Ampère fixes that average whatever the field looks like. The average does depend on the path, though:

looplengthaverage H
along the window's edge77.2 mm51.8 A/m
mean path100 mm40.0 A/m
along the core's outer edge122.8 mm32.6 A/m

Energy. Select every region (Operation → Block, select all), then Integrate → Magnetic field energy: W = 22.6 µJ. From W = ½ L i², L = 2W/i² = 4.53 mH, the same as step 6.

Mesh. Make the triangles smaller and solve again. If L barely moves, the mesh was fine enough.

Why 13 % higher?

4.53 / 4.02 = 1.13, because each turn has 13 % more flux through it than the formula assumes. There are two reasons:

  1. The flux takes the shorter inner path (step 5). The core carries about 11 % more flux, as if its path were about 90 mm instead of 100 mm. L goes as 1/ℓ, and 100/90 ≈ 1.11. Datasheets call this 90 mm the effective length ℓe. You can see it in the unwound right leg, which carries 11.16 µWb against the formula's 10.05.
  2. Leakage across the window. The wound leg carries 11.32 µWb, but only 11.16 µWb reaches the right leg. The other 1.5 % crosses the window through the air and comes back. It still passes through every turn, so it still adds to λ.

Together: 1.110 × 1.015 = 1.126.

What this 2D model leaves out

What "planar" assumes. FEMM solves the single cut you drew and assumes every other cut, at any depth into the page, looks exactly the same. It is like a loaf of bread that is the same slice all the way through. The real core is only 16.7 mm deep and has a front face and a back face, and two things happen there that the 2D model cannot show.

  1. The end turns. A real turn is a closed loop. It goes into the page through the window, crosses behind the leg at the back face, comes out of the page beside the leg's outer face, and crosses in front of the leg at the front face. The 2D cut only sees the two places where the wire passes through it: the two copper strips. The crossings at the front and back (the copper in the picture above) are missing from the model. They are short, but their current makes a little extra field in the air in front of and behind the core.
  2. The core's front and back faces. The 2D model behaves as if the core went on forever into the page, so no flux can leave through a front or back face. In the real core a little flux does: it bulges out of those faces into the air, most of all near the window, where the leakage field is.

Both add a little flux in the air that still passes through the turns, so the real L is slightly higher than the 2D answer. For this ungapped core the effect is small. Almost all the flux is inside the core, where every cut really does look the same. Checking the last few percent would take a 3D solve or a measurement.

Also left out: the core is linear, so there is no saturation, and the field is static, so there are no eddy currents.

Optional: scripting it in Python

The pyfemm package (pip install pyfemm) drives FEMM from Python, so the steps above can be a short script. An AI assistant can draft one for you. Trust its L only after the checks in step 7 and a comparison with the lecture's formula. The key lines:

import femm
femm.openfemm()
femm.newdocument(0)                                    # magnetics
femm.mi_probdef(0, "millimeters", "planar", 1e-8, 100/6, 30)
femm.mi_addmaterial("Core", 2000, 2000, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0)
femm.mi_addcircprop("coil", 0.1, 1)                    # 0.1 A, series
femm.mi_drawrectangle(0, 0, 35, 27)                    # core outline, mm
femm.mi_drawrectangle(6, 6, 29, 21)                    # window
# ... copper strips, block labels (turns -40 and +40), open boundary ...
femm.mi_analyze(1)
femm.mi_loadsolution()
current, voltage, flux_linkage = femm.mo_getcircuitproperties("coil")
print("L =", flux_linkage / current, "H")              # about 4.53e-3
